source_title: Inflation in India: A Pricey Background Reader - Frontline Magazine
source_excerpt:
A shopkeeper counts Indian currency coins at his shop in the old quarters of Delhi on September 24, 2025. | Photo Credit: ANUSHREE FADNAVIS/REUTERS
India’s retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September 2026, with food inflation climbing to 7.74 per cent. Wholesale inflation surged to 11.39 per cent, driven partly by rising energy prices amid the US-Israel war on Iran. The country’s inflation story is inseparable from the pressures on household budgets and the choices made by governments and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). In 2022-23, the war in Ukraine intensified global commodity shocks, adding to domestic price pressures. In subsequent years, vegetable and pulse prices repeatedly drove food inflation, complicating the RBI’s task of controlling prices through interest rates. By late 2025, a sharp fall in food prices had brought headline inflation down, offering relief after a prolonged period of elevated inflation. The latest figures underline the renewed urgency of these questions.
Food prices have repeatedly surged because of erratic weather, crop losses, and supply disruptions, while global oil prices and a weakening rupee have exposed the economy’s dependence on imported energy. The burden falls most heavily on poorer households, for whom food and transport consume a substantial share of monthly income.
This Frontline archive package traces the forces behind the country’s inflation problem, from the causes of rising prices and the politics of economic management to the rupee’s depreciation, industrial policy, and the country’s energy vulnerability. The articles also consider the consequences for economic growth and the credibility of official economic data. Together, they offer a historical perspective on an issue that continues to shape India’s economic choices and the everyday experience of its citizens.
